question.prompt: Design an API Rate Limiter to protect public endpoints from abuse and DoS attacks.
expectedPoints: Functional requirements (client identifier, throttling rules, headers returned)
Rate limiting algorithms (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window Counter)
Low-latency distributed storage (Redis with sorted sets or Lua scripts for atomicity)
Graceful degradation when rate limiter fails (fail-open vs fail-closed)
commonMistakes: Querying SQL database on every incoming HTTP request
Ignoring race conditions between parallel requests
Not specifying return codes (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests)

transcript: Candidate: To limit requests, every time a request comes into our API gateway, we insert a row into a Postgres table with user_id and timestamp. Then we run SELECT COUNT(*) FROM requests WHERE user_id = ? AND timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL 1 MINUTE. If the count is over 100, we throw an error. Interviewer: How does this perform under 50,000 requests per second across 10 regions? Candidate: Postgres is very fast. We can add an index on user_id. If Postgres gets slow, maybe we can put a cache in front of it somehow, but I don't know how the cache would count requests.
notes: Catastrophic architecture: SQL insert and count per request on high-throughput gateway. No knowledge of Token Bucket or Redis Lua scripts.
